cards.title: Does a fixed d-to-1 Games conjecture imply Unique Games?
cards.area: Approximation algorithms and hardness of approximation
cards.formal:
Is the following implication true for the classical constraint games and deterministic polynomial reductions defined below?
\[\bigl(\exists\,d\in\mathbb N,\ d\ge2\text{ and }D_d\bigr)\ \Longrightarrow\ \mathrm{UGC}.\]
Here \(D_d\) is the perfect-completeness \(d\)-to-one Games conjecture with \(d\) fixed independently of the soundness parameter; \(\mathrm{UGC}\) is the full near-perfect-completeness Unique Games conjecture. Equivalently, for every fixed \(d\ge2\), does \(D_d\) imply \(\mathrm{UGC}\)? The card retains the forward implication singled out in the saved source excerpt.

cards.definitions:
A constraint game has two finite disjoint vertex sets \(U,V\) and a nonempty finite list of edges \(e=(u_e,v_e)\in U\times V\). Repeated edges, with their own constraints, are allowed and count separately. Every edge has equal weight in the list. No regularity or bounded-degree promise is imposed. All vertices, edges and constraint tables are explicitly encoded with binary integers; there is no succinct representation or compressed multiplicity.

For integers \(d\ge2\) and \(r\ge1\), a \(d\)-to-one game gives left vertices labels in \([dr]\), right vertices labels in \([r]\), and every edge a surjective map \(\pi_e:[dr]\to[r]\) with exactly \(d\) preimages of every right label. Here \([m]=\{1,\ldots,m\}\). An assignment is a pair of maps \(\alpha:U\to[dr]\) and \(\beta:V\to[r]\); it satisfies edge \(e\) when \(\pi_e(\alpha(u_e))=\beta(v_e)\). Its value is the fraction of list entries it satisfies. The optimum \(\operatorname{val}(G)\) is the maximum of this fraction over all assignments. It lies in \([0,1]\) and is a finite rational maximum. Perfect completeness means the YES instance has optimum exactly one.

A Unique Game has the same bipartite constraint format, a common alphabet \([k]\) on both sides, and a permutation \(\pi_e:[k]\to[k]\) on each edge. Assignment, satisfaction and optimum are defined by the same equality. This is a classical combinatorial optimum; no entangled, interactive, nonsignalling or quantum strategy is used.

For a promised pair of disjoint YES and NO sets of such instances, NP-hard means that Boolean 3-SAT has a deterministic polynomial-time many-one reduction to that pair. Specifically, a single finite Turing program maps every explicitly encoded Boolean formula in conjunctive normal form with at most three literals per clause to a valid game. It maps satisfiable formulas into YES and unsatisfiable formulas into NO and uses at most \(K(L+1)^c\) bit steps on every length-\(L\) input, for fixed constants \(K,c\). Literal indices, signs, clauses, vertex names and table entries use ordinary explicit binary encodings. An algorithm for the promised game need have no specified behaviour outside YES and NO. NP-hardness here asserts the existence of a reduction; it does not assume \(\mathrm P\ne\mathrm{NP}\).

For a fixed integer \(d\ge2\), define \(D_d\) to mean:
\[\forall\gamma\in\mathbb Q\cap(0,1),\ \exists r\ge1:
\quad \operatorname{GapD}_{d,r}(1,\gamma)\text{ is NP-hard},\]
where the YES condition is \(\operatorname{val}(G)=1\) and the NO condition is \(\operatorname{val}(G)\le\gamma\). The integer \(d\) is outside the quantifier over \(\gamma\). The alphabet size \(r\), reduction program and its polynomial constants may depend on \(d,\gamma\), but not on the formula length. Allowing \(d\) to increase as \(\gamma\) decreases would be a different antecedent.

Define full \(\mathrm{UGC}\) by
\[\forall\eta,\gamma\in\mathbb Q\cap(0,1/4),\ \exists k\ge1:
\quad \operatorname{GapUG}_{k}(1-\eta,\gamma)\text{ is NP-hard}.\]
Its YES condition is \(\operatorname{val}(G)\ge1-\eta\) and its NO condition is \(\operatorname{val}(G)\le\gamma\). The constants \(k\) and the polynomial reduction may depend on both gap parameters. The rational, small-gap convention gives disjoint promises and is equivalent to requesting all arbitrarily small positive gaps: smaller rational gaps imply the less stringent real gaps. There is no demand for one alphabet or one polynomial degree working for all gap choices, or for a uniform algorithm generating all the reductions from their parameters.

The target is the implication between these mathematical hardness propositions. It is not a question about formal unprovability in a separately chosen axiom system, nor is it limited to one specified family of gadget or oracle reductions. The reverse implication from UGC to perfect-completeness \(d\)-to-one hardness is a separate question mentioned in the source, not an additional requirement on this card.
cards.answer_criterion: Give a complete Lean-checked proof or refutation of the displayed implication. An affirmative answer must establish full UGC from the assumption that \(D_d\) holds for some fixed \(d\ge2\), respecting the gap quantifiers and the deterministic polynomial reductions. An unconditional proof of UGC would also establish the implication. A negative answer must prove the conjunction \((\exists d\ge2\ D_d)\land\neg\mathrm{UGC}\); showing only that a particular reduction loses completeness, or that some restricted reduction class cannot work, does not refute the implication. Hardness of Unique Games with a fixed YES value such as \(1/d\) or \(1/2\) is not the required near-one YES value for every \(\eta>0\). Exact asymptotic proof is required; the numerical approximation tolerance does not alter these logical statements.

context_blocks.text: Both games ask for globally consistent labels subject to local compatibility rules. Unique Games has one allowed right label for each left label and also one allowed left label for each right label. A d-to-one constraint keeps the first property but permits d compatible left labels for a given right label. This additional freedom changes which perfect-completeness gaps are possible.

The source already proves a weaker implication: its Appendix B gives one-sided Unique Games hardness with completeness 1/d. This is one fixed positive completeness constant. Full UGC instead requires a YES value arbitrarily close to one while keeping soundness arbitrarily close to zero. The weaker implication therefore does not answer the source question.

Perfectly satisfiable Unique Games can be checked efficiently by trying a starting label in each connected component and propagating the forced labels. The conjecture deliberately permits a small positive fraction of unsatisfied constraints in the YES case. Substituting exact satisfiability for near-satisfiability would change the problem.

The 2025 journal account explains the sequence that proved almost-perfect-completeness two-to-one hardness. It retains exact perfect completeness as a separate conjecture and states full UGC separately. These distinctions matter even though all the parameters may be described informally as almost satisfiable games.

Fei, Minzer and Wang’s 14 September 2026 preprint claims perfect-completeness four-to-one hardness for every positive soundness constant. If correct, its Theorem 1.6 establishes D₄ and hence the antecedent of this card. Under that theorem, the forward implication is equivalent to UGC itself: an implication proof would give UGC, while UGC immediately implies the implication. This is a logical consequence of the claimed theorem, not a claim that UGC has been proved. The new full proof has not been independently audited here.

This connection would turn a hardness theorem with several compatible labels into the general Unique Games hypothesis underlying many sharp approximation thresholds. Keeping alphabet size, constraint multiplicity, completeness and soundness explicit prevents a useful weaker hardness theorem from being mistaken for that conclusion.

context_blocks.title: Buying fractions of directed arcs
context_blocks.text: A tour buys each used arc completely. The relaxation permits fractional amounts of several arcs, while requiring one unit to enter and leave every city and at least one unit to leave every proper group of cities. Every tour is feasible for the LP, so the LP gives a lower bound on the tour cost. The quantity measures the largest possible multiplicative loss when converting fractional cost into an actual tour; the classical conjecture sets that loss at two. A fractional solution need not be a probability distribution over whole tours.

context_blocks.title: Why subtour constraints matter
context_blocks.text: Suppose six cities form two groups of three, with travel cost 1 within a group and 10 between groups. Two separate three-city directed cycles satisfy every degree condition and cost only 6, but do not form a tour visiting all cities. The cut inequality for either group rules out this disconnected solution. These inequalities therefore add a global requirement to the local degree constraints; whether that requirement is strong enough to keep the full gap at two is the unresolved issue.

context_blocks.title: The current general gap
context_blocks.text: Families of directed instances have ratios tending to 2, so no smaller universal factor can work. Traub and Vygen’s 2022 article establishes an upper bound of 22. Their 2024 book improves the proved bound to 17 and explicitly retains the factor-2 question. Its circulation LP has the same optimum as the degree-constrained LP on directed metrics, so the model matches this card. The book also notes room for a small further numerical improvement; 17 is a stated theorem, not a claim that no refinement exists.

context_blocks.title: Finite computations and half-integral vertices
context_blocks.text: Vercesi and coauthors construct improved lower-bound instances at particular sizes. The June 2026 revision by Sosso, Bernardelli and Gualandi computes the gaps for all half-integral extreme points through twelve vertices, where half-integral means coordinates in \(\{0,1/2,1\}\). An extreme point is a feasible LP solution that cannot be written as a nontrivial convex combination of two distinct feasible solutions. Other denominators and arbitrarily large instances remain outside that enumeration. These computations add evidence without proving the universal conjecture.

context_blocks.title: What a resolution would establish
context_blocks.text: The comparison measures the strength of this specific relaxation. A polynomial-time method achieving cost at most twice the LP optimum would settle the inequality and give an approximation guarantee, but the existence inequality itself does not promise an efficient construction. The symmetric metric TSP has a different classical \(4/3\) conjecture; its constants and finite verifications do not transfer to the larger family in which travel costs can depend on direction.

cards.title: Constant-factor approximation for uniform Sparsest Cut
cards.area: Approximation algorithms and hardness of approximation
cards.formal: Do a universal \(C\ge 1\) and a randomized polynomial-time algorithm exist which, on every finite simple undirected graph G on \(n\ge 2\) vertices, output a nonempty proper set S with \(\varphi _{G}(S)\le C \min _{\varnothing \ne T\subsetneq V} \varphi _{G}(T)\), with probability at least \(2/3\)?
cards.definitions: Here \(\varphi _{G}(S)=|E(S,V\setminus S)|/(|S|\cdot |V\setminus S|)\), where \(E(S,V\setminus S)\) is the set of edges having exactly one endpoint in S. The graph is supplied explicitly by an adjacency matrix. Polynomial time is measured in bit operations on every random tape; the same algorithm and constant must work for all graphs. The zero-optimum disconnected case requires returning a zero cut. Uniform refers to equal demand for each pair of vertices, not regularity of the graph.

context_blocks.text: Uniform Sparsest Cut balances a cut’s edge boundary against the number of separated pairs. It is a basic measure of the decomposability of a graph and a major test case for approximation algorithms.

The ARV result gives an \(O(\sqrt{\log  n})\) approximation, with a bound growing with the graph size. A constant factor would cross the remaining qualitative approximation barrier. Nonuniform pair demands, conductance normalized by volumes, and Small-Set Expansion have different targets and are not silently substituted here.

cards.title: Constant-factor approximation for Dasgupta’s hierarchical clustering objective
cards.area: Approximation algorithms and hardness of approximation
cards.formal: Do there exist real constants \(C\ge1\), \(K>0\), an integer \(a\ge1\), and one deterministic multitape Turing machine which, on every explicitly encoded nonnegative rational similarity graph \(G\), outputs a hierarchy \(T\) with \(\operatorname{cost}_G(T)\le C\operatorname{OPT}(G)\) within \(K(N+1)^a\) bit operations, where \(N\) is the total input bit length and the cost and allowed hierarchies are defined below?
cards.definitions:
An input is an integer \(n\ge2\) and a finite simple undirected graph \(G=([n],E,w)\), where \([n]=\{1,\ldots,n\}\), \(E\subseteq\{\{u,v\}:1\le u<v\le n\}\), and \(w:E\to\mathbb Q_{\ge0}\). The encoding explicitly lists all \(n\) vertices, including isolated ones, and all edges with their endpoints and weights. Integers use ordinary binary notation with delimiters; each rational weight is a nonnegative integer numerator and positive integer denominator in binary. The explicit vertex list ensures \(N\ge n\). There are no loops or repeated edges. An absent edge has weight zero. The graph need not be connected and has no metric, clusterability, density or sampling promise.

A hierarchy is a finite rooted full binary tree whose leaves are labeled bijectively by \([n]\); every internal node has exactly two children. For a node \(z\), let \(L_T(z)\subseteq[n]\) be its descendant leaf labels. For distinct leaves \(u,v\), let \(\operatorname{lca}_T(u,v)\) be their least common ancestor. Define
\[
\operatorname{cost}_G(T)=\sum_{\{u,v\}\in E}w(\{u,v\})\,|L_T(\operatorname{lca}_T(u,v))|,
\qquad
\operatorname{OPT}(G)=\min_T\operatorname{cost}_G(T).
\]
Each unordered edge contributes once. The minimum is over all such trees, with no restriction on height or balance. The output explicitly lists the root, child edges and leaf labels of one tree. If all weights are zero, the required cost is zero and any valid hierarchy qualifies.

The same finite machine and constants must work for every \(n\), graph and weight encoding. All input reads, binary arithmetic, preprocessing and output writes count in the worst-case running time. The machine has no random bits, advice, external comparison or cluster-label oracle, or uncharged preprocessing. The factor \(C\) is independent of \(n\), the number of edges and the sizes or ratios of the weights; it is not an input parameter. Only the tree is required as output, and its stated cost guarantee is mathematical, using exact rational weights.

context_blocks.text: The source defines a cost for a complete hierarchy of pairwise similarities. This card retains the previously selected deterministic polynomial-time, constant-factor question. The explicit rational encoding and vertex list fix bit complexity and output size; they do not impose a structural promise.

The general approximation guarantee of Charikar and Chatziafratis is \(O(\sqrt{\log n})\). Their Theorem 3.4 proves Small-Set-Expansion hardness of approximation within every constant factor, already on unweighted graphs. This is a conditional complexity barrier, not an unconditional proof that the requested machine cannot exist.
The ICALP 2025 sublinear result assumes a clusterable graph and access to cluster labels of sampled seeds. Its input model and guarantee do not supply the unrestricted algorithm asked for here.

The July 2026 generalized clustering paper permits a leaf cluster to remain a whole graph from a specified class, such as a tree. Its objective can consequently vanish on inputs for which singleton-leaf hierarchies have positive cost. Those results concern a different stopping rule.

A constant-factor guarantee for the complementary revenue-maximization objective does not, just from that guarantee, give a constant-factor bound for this minimization objective. The target here is the displayed cost itself.

cards.why: A hierarchy must represent similarity at every scale, so optimizing a single flat partition is insufficient. A constant approximation for this canonical objective would give a uniform quality guarantee on arbitrary similarity data and would cross a major graph-partitioning hardness barrier.
cards.answer_criterion: Supply a complete mathematically correct Lean proof of the existence of a machine and fixed constants satisfying every stated guarantee, or a complete Lean proof of their nonexistence. An approximation factor growing with the input size, a result for a promised graph class, or a guarantee with an additional oracle does not settle this target. A conditional hardness result establishes its implication but does not by itself prove the unconditional negative answer.

cards.title: Min-CSP approximation at the SDP integrality gap
cards.area: Approximation algorithms and hardness of approximation
cards.formal:
For every fixed finite domain \(D\), positive arity \(k\), and finite set \(\Lambda\) of nonnegative rational cost functions \(f:D^k\to[0,1]\), is the following true? For every rational \(\varepsilon>0\), there is a randomized polynomial-time algorithm which, on every \(n\)-variable minimization \(\Lambda\)-CSP instance \(I\) with finite \(n\)-variable SDP integrality gap \(\alpha_\Lambda(n)\), returns an assignment \(\sigma\) such that
\[\Pr\bigl[\operatorname{cost}_I(\sigma)\leq (1+\varepsilon)\alpha_\Lambda(n)\operatorname{OPT}(I)\bigr]\geq\tfrac23?\]
The same algorithm handles all \(n\); it also halts and returns an assignment on the sizes where the gap is infinite, but no multiplicative guarantee is imposed there. The gap and the basic SDP are defined below.
cards.why: A universal theorem would extend the general SDP approximation framework to multiplicative minimization guarantees, including instances whose optimum vanishes with input size. It would connect a geometric obstruction of a standard relaxation to actual polynomial-time approximation across all finite cost languages. A counterexample would identify a limit to interpreting integrality gaps as achievable algorithmic benchmarks.
cards.status_note: The 2017 chapter explicitly poses this n-dependent multiplicative question after distinguishing it from the 2009 additive rounding theorem. sentences: A minimization CSP assigns finite-domain values to variables to minimize the average of fixed local nonnegative costs.
Its basic SDP can achieve a lower cost using consistent local distributions and vectors than any actual assignment.
The question asks whether a randomized polynomial-time algorithm can match the SDP’s worst gap at each number of variables within every factor 1+ε.
The multiplicative guarantee must also protect zero or very small optimum values, which existing additive universal rounding does not do.
A resolution would clarify whether size-dependent SDP gaps universally predict achievable approximation for minimization CSPs.

cards.definitions:
Fix \(D=\{1,\ldots,q\}\), with \(q\geq1\), and a finite nonempty \(\Lambda\). Its rational cost tables and \(k\geq1\) are fixed, not input. The nonnegative rational convention gives a finite effective version of the source’s generalized nonnegative predicates; negative costs do not define the multiplicative approximation question. An instance has variables \(x_1,\ldots,x_n\), \(n\geq1\), and a finite list of \(m\) constraints \(C=(f_C,(i_1,\ldots,i_k))\). Every \(f_C\in\Lambda\), and each \(i_j\in[n]\). Repeated coordinates and repeated occurrences are allowed, with each occurrence having unit weight. There are no hard constraints, infinite costs, extra unary pins or input-dependent predicates. For an assignment \(\sigma:[n]\to D\), set
\[\operatorname{cost}_I(\sigma)=\frac1m\sum_C f_C(\sigma(i_1),\ldots,\sigma(i_k)),\qquad \operatorname{OPT}(I)=\min_\sigma\operatorname{cost}_I(\sigma).\]
For \(m=0\), cost and optimum are zero. A zero-one cost table records violation by value one and satisfaction by value zero. Different arities can be represented by a common maximum arity with unused arguments; the question is not restricted to Boolean predicates.

Define the basic semidefinite relaxation as follows. Choose real vectors \(v_0,u_{i,a}\in\mathbb R^{1+nq}\), for \(i\in[n],a\in D\), satisfying
\[\langle v_0,v_0\rangle=1,\qquad \sum_{a\in D}u_{i,a}=v_0,\qquad \langle u_{i,a},u_{i,b}\rangle=0\quad(a\ne b).\]
For each constraint occurrence \(C\), let \(S_C\) be its set of distinct variables and choose a local distribution \(\mu_C:D^{S_C}\to\mathbb R_{\geq0}\) with total mass one. Impose
\[\sum_{z:z(i)=a}\mu_C(z)=\langle u_{i,a},u_{i,a}\rangle\quad(i\in S_C),\]
\[\sum_{z:z(i)=a,\ z(j)=b}\mu_C(z)=\langle u_{i,a},u_{j,b}\rangle\quad(i,j\in S_C,\ i\ne j).\]
Thus all local one- and two-variable marginals agree with the common vector inner products. Repeated occurrences of a variable in a constraint use the same value \(z(i)\). The SDP value \(\operatorname{SDP}(I)\) is the minimum of
\[\frac1m\sum_C\sum_{z\in D^{S_C}}\mu_C(z)f_C(z(i_1),\ldots,z(i_k)),\]
with value zero when \(m=0\). This is a finite semidefinite program via its Gram matrix; the stated vector dimension suffices for every such matrix. It is feasible and compact in Gram-matrix and distribution coordinates. Every assignment gives a feasible point, so \(0\leq\operatorname{SDP}(I)\leq\operatorname{OPT}(I)\). No higher level of an SDP hierarchy is included.

For a fixed instance define its gap ratio as \(\operatorname{OPT}(I)/\operatorname{SDP}(I)\) if the denominator is positive, as one if both values are zero, and as \(+\infty\) if only the denominator is zero. Let \(\alpha_\Lambda(n)\) be the supremum of these ratios over all lists of constraints on exactly \(n\) labelled variables; unused variables are counted. Then \(1\leq\alpha_\Lambda(n)\leq+\infty\), and the gap may grow with \(n\). The algorithm is not supplied with its value or an oracle for it. This is an instance-size gap, not a single constant supremum over every size.

Encode \(n,m\) in unary and each constraint by its fixed-table index and its \(k\) variable indices in binary; the total bit length is \(L\). The algorithm is a finite probabilistic multitape Turing machine using independent fair coin bits. For each fixed \(D,k,\Lambda,\varepsilon\), one program has worst-case running time \(C(L+1)^c\) on every input and every coin sequence; \(C,c\) may depend on these fixed parameters. Malformed strings may be rejected. The output explicitly gives all \(n\) labels. No polynomial dependence on \(1/\varepsilon\), common exponent across languages or effective algorithm for finding the program from \(\Lambda\) is required. The probability convention is the explicit bounded-error interpretation of the source’s randomized approximation framework.

The guarantee is multiplicative, relative to the actual optimum. When that optimum is zero and the size-dependent gap is finite, the algorithm must find a zero-cost assignment with probability at least \(2/3\). There is no additive error term, and no assertion that it must round a supplied SDP point or achieve the stronger bound with \(\operatorname{SDP}(I)\) in place of \(\operatorname{OPT}(I)\).
cards.answer_criterion: Give a complete mathematically correct proof checked in Lean of the universal algorithmic assertion, or of its logical negation. A positive proof must establish one polynomial-time machine for every fixed language and positive accuracy, working at all input sizes with the stated success probability, size-dependent gap and zero-optimum convention. A negative proof must establish a fixed finite language and positive accuracy for which no such machine exists. A constant additive guarantee for normalized cost, an algorithm restricted to one predicate family, or a conditional obstruction to one rounding scheme does not settle the universal statement. An unproved complexity assumption may support partial progress but is not part of this unconditional target.

source_formulation.text: If the minimization SDP gap at n variables is α_n, can a polynomial-time algorithm attain approximation factor (1+ε)α_n for every positive ε?
source_formulation.caption: Editorial paraphrase of Chapter 11, §7, Open Problem 4; the n-dependent gap is retained, with finite cost encoding, zero cases and success probability made explicit.

context_blocks.text: The integrality gap measures a relaxation’s worst discrepancy from a genuine assignment. In minimization, the SDP can make local constraints appear cheaper than any global assignment. This question asks whether an efficient algorithm can always match the resulting size-dependent benchmark to arbitrarily small relative slack; it does not ask to compute the gap itself.

The source distinguishes maximization and minimization with nonnegative predicates. For maximization, a random assignment provides a positive baseline for each nonzero fixed predicate, allowing additive approximation losses to become relative losses. For minimization, satisfiable or nearly satisfiable instances can have optimum zero or arbitrarily close to zero, so the same argument fails.

Raghavendra and Steurer’s universal rounding theorem obtains the integrality-gap curve with an additive error in both its argument and its returned objective. Its running-time dependence on that additive accuracy can be very large. Taking the accuracy to shrink with the instance size therefore does not yield the polynomial-time multiplicative guarantee asked here.

The source explicitly permits α_n to depend on n. Replacing it by one global constant would discard major minimization examples, while a generic additive approximation to a normalized objective would leave zero and very small costs unprotected. These are essential parts of the question, not presentation choices.

The 2026 robust-satisfiability work obtains quantitative guarantees for specified majority and plurality preservation classes, along with separate conditional hardness for a particular promise problem. Those results concern selected families and loss curves. They do not assert a universal algorithm matching the exact n-variable multiplicative SDP gap for every finite nonnegative cost language.

cards.title: Square-root logarithmic approximation for metric labeling
cards.area: Approximation algorithms and hardness of approximation
cards.formal: Does a randomized polynomial-time algorithm exist giving an \(O(\sqrt{\log (k+2)})\) approximation for every metric-labeling instance with k labels?
cards.definitions: An instance consists of a finite undirected graph \(G=(V,E)\), nonnegative rational edge weights \(w_{uv}, a\) metric d on \([k]\) supplied by its rational distance matrix, and nonnegative rational assignment costs \(c(v,i)\). A labeling \(f:V\to [k]\) has cost \(\sum_{v} c(v,f(v))+\sum_{uv\in E}w_{uv} d(f(u),f(v))\). The guarantee is \(\operatorname{cost}(f)\le C\sqrt{\log (k+2)}\cdot\)OPT with probability at least \(2/3\) for a universal C. Running time on every random tape is polynomial in the entire binary input length; k is part of the input. No restriction on the metric or graph is promised.

context_blocks.text: Metric labeling combines local assignment costs with penalties for assigning far-apart labels to neighboring vertices. It captures a broad family of classification and partitioning objectives.

General algorithms give logarithmic approximation, while the square-root logarithmic scale arises in hardness. Closing the gap would identify the approximation power of this general model. Results for a uniform, line or truncated metric leave arbitrary label metrics unresolved.

cards.definitions: A digraph \(D=(V,A)\) has labeled vertex set \(V=\{1,\ldots ,n\}\), no loops, and at most one arc in each direction between distinct vertices; opposite arcs are allowed. Its binary encoding explicitly lists vertices and arcs. A directed cycle has at least two distinct vertices \(v_{1},\ldots ,v_{\ell}\) and arcs \(v_{i}\to v_{i+1}\), with indices modulo \(\ell\). A k-dicoloring is a map \(c:V\to \{1,\ldots ,k\}\) such that each color class induces an acyclic digraph, equivalently no directed cycle is monochromatic. The dichromatic number is the least k admitting such a map. The promise problem for k accepts inputs with dichromatic number at most 2 and rejects those with dichromatic number greater than k; inputs with values \(3,\ldots ,k\) are outside the promise. The NP-hardness claim means that for each fixed k there is a deterministic algorithm \(R_{k}\) and constants \(c_{k},C_{k}\) such that, on a 3-CNF formula F of bit length \(N, R_{k}\) outputs a digraph in time at most \(C_{k}(N+1)^{c}_{k}\), with satisfiable F mapped to the accepting side and unsatisfiable F mapped to the rejecting side. A 3-CNF is a conjunction of clauses of at most three literals, each a variable or its negation. The reduction and its polynomial may depend on k, but not on F or N; k is not an input-size parameter. A promised coloring algorithm is given the graph without a 2-coloring and must return a valid k-dicoloring. A gap reduction of the stated kind rules out such a polynomial-time algorithm unless \(\mathrm{P}=\mathrm{NP}\), since validity of an output coloring can be checked in polynomial time.
cards.answer_criterion: Prove the stated NP-hardness for every fixed \(k\ge 4\), or refute that universal hardness assertion. A polynomial-time k-coloring algorithm for some fixed k would contradict the claim under \(\mathrm{P}\ne \mathrm{NP}\). Hardness for \(k=3\), bounds for a growing number of colors, or hardness without the two-colorability completeness promise do not suffice.

context_blocks.text: In a directed path \(u\to v\to w\), all three vertices may receive the same color because there is no directed cycle. cards.definitions: A binary constraint satisfaction instance has k variables, a finite alphabet \(\Sigma\) of size n, and explicitly given binary relations specifying the allowed pairs for constrained variable pairs. Its finite input length includes these relation tables. An assignment chooses one alphabet value for each variable; \(\operatorname{val}(\Pi )\) is the maximum fraction of its constraints satisfied by an assignment. The promise is \(\operatorname{val}(\Pi )=1\) or \(\operatorname{val}(\Pi )\le 1- \varepsilon\); no answer is prescribed for intermediate values. For an instance of encoded size L, fixed-parameter tractable means time \(f(k)\mathrm{L}^{C}\) for some computable f and constant C independent of k and L. In the standard representation with one binary relation per constrained pair, this is equivalent to \(f(k)n^{O(1)}\) after absorbing polynomial k-factors into f. Here \(\mathrm{W}[1]\ne \mathrm{FPT}\) is the standard deterministic hypothesis, equivalently that deciding whether a finite graph has a k-clique has no \(f(k)\mathrm{L}^{C}\) algorithm. PIH asserts the existence of one fixed \(\varepsilon >0\) for which the promised approximation task has no such algorithm, irrespective of the computable function f or constant exponent C. The question is the implication from exact parameterized hardness to that constant-gap hardness, not an unconditional assertion of \(\mathrm{W}[1]\ne \mathrm{FPT}\).
cards.answer_criterion: Establish the stated implication using only \(\mathrm{W}[1]\ne \mathrm{FPT}\) as the complexity assumption, with a constant gap independent of k and n, or refute that implication. A result assuming ETH or Gap-ETH, a gap shrinking with k, or hardness for a list-assignment variant does not settle this target.

cards.definitions: G is a finite nonempty simple undirected graph, represented by its adjacency matrix or edge list. An independent set is a set of vertices containing no edge; \(\alpha (G)\) is its maximum size. The subgraph induced by \(U\subseteq V(G)\) contains all edges of G with both endpoints in U. It is properly 3-colorable if a map \(U\to \{1,2,3\}\) gives adjacent vertices different labels. Define iCol\(_{3}(G)=N^{- 1}\max\){|\(U|:G[U]\) is 3-colorable}. The yes case is iCol\(_{3}(G)\ge 1- \eta\), and the no case is \(\alpha (G)/N<\varepsilon\). Fractions refer to vertices, not edges or color classes of a fixed coloring. The parameters \(\varepsilon ,\eta\) are fixed before the reduction and are not part of the graph input. In the usual deterministic NP-hardness formulation, for each pair there must be a deterministic polynomial-time map from Boolean satisfiability instances to graphs that sends satisfiable inputs into the yes case and unsatisfiable inputs into the no case. The polynomial may depend on \(\varepsilon\) and \(\eta\). An algorithm for the promise problem may behave arbitrarily on graphs in neither case. Since a 3-colorable set has an independent subset of at least one third its size, the displayed parameter restriction ensures disjoint cases. The paper’s already proved weaker theorem allows randomized reductions; that distinction must be retained when assessing a claimed resolution.
cards.answer_criterion: Prove the stated gap NP-hardness for every fixed admissible \(\varepsilon ,\eta\), with a reduction and its completeness and soundness guarantees, or refute the universal hardness assertion. If a claimed hardness result uses randomized reductions, state that convention explicitly and distinguish it from deterministic NP-hardness. A polynomial-time algorithm would contradict the deterministic hardness claim under \(\mathrm{P}\ne \mathrm{NP}\); without a complexity separation, it alone is not a logical refutation of NP-hardness.
